title: Collaborative Filtering: Recommending from the Table Alone

collaborative filtering.markdown: Predicting what a user will like from the ratings of **many** users — no content features needed. Neighborhood methods borrow from similar users or items; latent-factor methods embed users and items in a shared space where a rating is a dot product.
collaborative filtering.prompt: Explain collaborative filtering: what problem it solves, why it needs no item features, and the difference between neighborhood and latent-factor methods.

rating matrix.markdown: $R \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, users by items, with $r_{ui}$ known only on a small observed set $\Omega$. The Netflix Prize matrix was about $1.2\%$ filled.
rating matrix.prompt: Explain the rating matrix in collaborative filtering and why its sparsity is the central difficulty.

observed set.markdown: $\Omega = \{(u,i) : r_{ui} \text{ is known}\}$. Matrix factorization fits only these entries; a missing rating is **unknown**, not zero.
observed set.prompt: Explain the observed set Omega and why matrix factorization sums its loss only over observed entries.

Pearson similarity.markdown: $w_{uv} = \dfrac{\sum_{i}(r_{ui}-\bar r_u)(r_{vi}-\bar r_v)}{\sqrt{\sum_i (r_{ui}-\bar r_u)^2}\sqrt{\sum_i (r_{vi}-\bar r_v)^2}}$ over co-rated items. Mean-centering removes each user's personal rating scale.
Pearson similarity.prompt: Explain Pearson similarity between users in collaborative filtering and why each user is centered on their own mean.

latent factor.markdown: A learned coordinate shared by users and items. A rating is predicted as $\hat r_{ui} = q_i^\top p_u$. The axes are not labeled genres: any invertible $A$ gives the same predictions via $(PA)(QA^{-\top})^\top = PQ^\top$.
latent factor.prompt: Explain latent factors in matrix factorization and why the learned axes are not genres.

matrix factorization.markdown: Approximate $R \approx PQ^\top$ with $P \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times k}$, $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$, fitted on $\Omega$ only with an $L_2$ penalty (Koren, Bell & Volinsky 2009).
matrix factorization.prompt: Explain matrix factorization for recommender systems: the model, the objective, and why it is low rank.

ALS.markdown: Fix $Q$ and every $p_u$ has a closed form, $p_u = (Q_{I_u}^\top Q_{I_u} + \lambda I)^{-1} Q_{I_u}^\top r_u$; then fix $P$ and solve for $Q$. Each half-step cannot increase the loss.
ALS.prompt: Explain alternating least squares for matrix factorization and derive the per-user update.

SGD.markdown: For each observed rating, $e = r_{ui} - q_i^\top p_u$, then $q_i \leftarrow q_i + \gamma(e\,p_u - \lambda q_i)$ and $p_u \leftarrow p_u + \gamma(e\,q_i - \lambda p_u)$. Popularized by Simon Funk in the Netflix Prize.
SGD.prompt: Explain stochastic gradient descent for matrix factorization and compare it with ALS.

regularization.markdown: The $\lambda(\lVert p_u\rVert^2 + \lVert q_i\rVert^2)$ term. With few ratings per user and many factors, the unregularized fit memorizes the training cells and extrapolates wildly to the hidden ones.
regularization.prompt: Explain why matrix factorization needs regularization and what happens without it.

cold start.markdown: A new user or item has too few ratings to pin down its $k$-dimensional vector: with fewer than $k$ ratings the least-squares system is underdetermined and only $\lambda$ keeps it finite.
cold start.prompt: Explain the cold-start problem in collaborative filtering and common remedies.

implicit feedback.markdown: Behavior such as views, clicks or plays instead of stars. There are no negative examples: an unwatched item may be disliked or just unseen. Hu, Koren & Volinsky (2008) model a binary preference with a confidence weight.
implicit feedback.prompt: Explain implicit feedback in recommender systems and why it needs a different model from explicit ratings.

confidence weight.markdown: $c_{ui} = 1 + \alpha\, r_{ui}$: how much the loss trusts preference $p_{ui}$. Every cell is fitted, unobserved ones as low-confidence zeros.
confidence weight.prompt: Explain the confidence weight c_ui = 1 + alpha r_ui in implicit-feedback matrix factorization.

RMSE.markdown: $\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{|T|}\sum_{(u,i)\in T}(r_{ui}-\hat r_{ui})^2}$ on a held-out set $T$. The Netflix Prize goal was a $10\%$ cut from Cinematch's $0.9525$ to $0.8572$.
RMSE.prompt: Explain RMSE as an evaluation metric for rating prediction and its role in the Netflix Prize.

scenes.title: The empty table
scenes.description: Six users, six movies, thirty known ratings and six blanks. Collaborative filtering is the art of filling the blanks from the table alone.
scenes.markdown:
# The empty table

A recommender sees a **rating matrix** $R$: one row per user $u$, one column per item $i$, and an entry $r_{ui}$ only where that user rated that item. Everything else is unknown.

## How empty is "empty"?

| Dataset | users | items | ratings | filled |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Netflix Prize (2006) | 480,189 | 17,770 | 100,480,507 | ≈ 1.2% |
| MovieLens 100K | 943 | 1,682 | 100,000 | ≈ 6.3% |
| This lesson's toy | 6 | 6 | 30 | 83% |

The toy is deliberately dense: six hidden ratings are enough to show every method succeeding and failing.

## The toy

The ratings were **designed**, not collected: each person and each movie was given a profile on three tastes — Action, Romance, Sci-fi — and every rating is the dot product of the two profiles (scene 3). That makes the table exactly *rank 3*, so a correct method can recover the hidden cells almost perfectly. Real data is noisy and never this clean.

## Training and test

$$\Omega = \{(u,i) : r_{ui}\ \text{observed}\}$$

Methods learn from $\Omega$ only. The six hidden cells are the **test set**, used only to grade, with

$$\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{|T|}\textstyle\sum_{(u,i)\in T}(r_{ui}-\hat r_{ui})^2}.$$

## Collaborative filtering

"Collaborative" because the prediction for you is built from *other people's* ratings — no plot summaries, no genres, no actors. The two classic families:

1. **Neighborhood methods** — Resnick et al., *GroupLens* (CSCW 1994); Sarwar et al., item-based CF (WWW 2001); Linden, Smith & York, Amazon item-to-item (IEEE Internet Computing 2003).
2. **Latent-factor models** — Koren, Bell & Volinsky, "Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems", *IEEE Computer* 42(8), 2009.

**Sources:** Netflix Prize rules and dataset statistics (Bennett & Lanning, KDD Cup 2007); Harper & Konstan, "The MovieLens Datasets", *ACM TiiS* 2015.

scenes.markdown:
# Neighbors: people who rate like you

## User-based collaborative filtering

The oldest recipe (Resnick et al., *GroupLens*, 1994): to predict $r_{ui}$, find users who have agreed with $u$ in the past and see what they thought of $i$.

### Similarity

Compare users only on items **both** rated, $I_{uv}$, after subtracting each user's mean $\bar r_u$:

$$w_{uv}=\frac{\sum_{i\in I_{uv}}(r_{ui}-\bar r_u)(r_{vi}-\bar r_v)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i\in I_{uv}}(r_{ui}-\bar r_u)^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_{i\in I_{uv}}(r_{vi}-\bar r_v)^2}}$$

This is the Pearson correlation — the cosine of the two **centered** rating vectors. Centering matters: a generous rater (everything 4–5) and a harsh one (everything 1–3) with identical taste get $w = 1$.

### Prediction

$$\hat r_{ui}=\bar r_u+\frac{\sum_{v\in N_i^n(u)} w_{uv}\,(r_{vi}-\bar r_v)}{\sum_{v\in N_i^n(u)}|w_{uv}|}$$

where $N_i^n(u)$ are the $n$ users most similar to $u$ **who rated $i$**. Each neighbor contributes how much more (or less) than *their own* average they liked $i$.

## In the toy

| | value |
|---|---|
| Dan's neighbors for *Die Hard* ($n=2$) | Ava ($w=0.89$), Eli ($w=0.80$) |
| prediction | 2.75 (truth 3) |
| test RMSE over the six hidden cells | 1.61 |

## Item-based CF

Sarwar et al. (WWW 2001) flipped the roles: similarity between **items**, using the *adjusted cosine* (subtract each **user's** mean), and predict from the user's own ratings of similar items:

$$\hat r_{ui}=\frac{\sum_{j\in N_u^n(i)} s_{ij}\,r_{uj}}{\sum_{j\in N_u^n(i)}|s_{ij}|}.$$

Items gather many more ratings than a typical user gives, so their similarities are stabler and can be precomputed — the basis of Amazon's item-to-item recommender (Linden, Smith & York, 2003).

## Why move on

Neighborhood methods need co-rated items, which sparse data rarely supplies; they scale with the number of users × items; and they never say **why** two people agree. Latent-factor models (next scene) answer the "why".

scenes.markdown:
# Taste space: a rating is a dot product

## Latent factors

Give every movie $i$ a vector $q_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$ and every user $u$ a vector $p_u \in \mathbb{R}^k$, and predict

$$\hat r_{ui} = q_i^{\top} p_u = \sum_{f=1}^{k} q_{if}\,p_{uf}.$$

Koren, Bell & Volinsky (2009) describe the factors as measuring "obvious dimensions such as comedy versus drama, amount of action, or orientation to children" — *or* "less well-defined dimensions … or completely uninterpretable dimensions". In this scene the three axes are **designed** to be readable (Action, Romance, Sci-fi); the algorithm in scene 5 is never told them.

## The toy, exactly

| | Action | Romance | Sci-fi |
|---|---|---|---|
| Die Hard | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| Notebook | 0 | 2 | 0 |
| Arrival | 0 | 0 | 2 |
| Mr & Mrs Smith | 2 | 2 | 0 |
| Matrix | 2 | 0 | 2 |
| Her | 0 | 2 | 2 |

Users: Ava $(2,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, Ben $(\tfrac12,2,\tfrac12)$, Cleo $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,2)$, Dan $(\tfrac32,1,\tfrac12)$, Eli $(1,1,1)$, Fay $(1,\tfrac12,\tfrac32)$. Every rating in scene 1 is one of these dot products.

## Angle and length

$$q_i^{\top}p_u = \lVert q_i\rVert\,\lVert p_u\rVert\cos\theta_{ui}$$

- $\cos\theta$ — **how well** the taste matches the content.
- $\lVert q_i\rVert$ — how strongly the movie expresses its ingredients. Two-genre movies here have length $2\sqrt2$, pure ones $2$, so the mixtures get higher scores from almost everyone. In learned models, item length correlates with **popularity**, which is one reason raw dot-product recommenders over-recommend popular items.
- $\lVert p_u\rVert$ — how emphatic the user is. It scales the user's whole row and never changes their ranking.

## Same geometry as attention

A transformer's attention score $q^{\top}k$ (see the *Transformer architecture* lesson) is the same object: a dot product between a "what I want" vector and a "what I offer" vector. Recommenders got there first.

scenes.markdown:
# $R \approx PQ^{\top}$: a low-rank table

## All dot products at once

With users as the rows of $P \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times k}$ and items as the rows of $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$,

$$\hat R = PQ^{\top}, \qquad \hat r_{ui} = q_i^{\top}p_u.$$

$\hat R$ has rank at most $k$. Matrix factorization **assumes** taste is explained by a few factors — in the Netflix Prize, models used $k$ from about 20 up to hundreds.

## Counting

A rank-$k$ $m\times n$ matrix has $(m+n)k - k^2$ degrees of freedom: $P$ and $Q$ hold $(m+n)k$ numbers, but $(PA)(QA^{-\top})^{\top} = PQ^{\top}$ for every invertible $k\times k$ matrix $A$, which removes $k^2$. For the toy, $12\cdot 3 - 9 = 27 \le 30 = |\Omega|$.

## Why not just take the SVD?

The Eckart–Young theorem says the best rank-$k$ approximation of a **fully known** matrix is its truncated SVD. Our matrix is not fully known, and

> "Conventional SVD is undefined when knowledge about the matrix is incomplete." — Koren, Bell & Volinsky (2009)

Filling the blanks with zeros makes it defined but wrong: the fit treats every unseen movie as hated. In the toy the hidden 5s come back as 0.77 and 0.60, and the test RMSE is **2.73** — worse than the neighborhood method.

## The objective

Score the model only where we have data, and penalize large vectors:

$$\min_{P,Q}\sum_{(u,i)\in\Omega}\big(r_{ui}-q_i^{\top}p_u\big)^2+\lambda\Big(\sum_u\lVert p_u\rVert^2+\sum_i\lVert q_i\rVert^2\Big).$$

This is Koren et al.'s Eq. 2 in the common per-vector form (they put $\lambda$ inside the sum over ratings, which penalizes busy users and items more); Eq. 5 adds the bias terms of scene 7. Simon Funk's 2006 blog post *"Netflix Update: Try This at Home"* popularized fitting it by stochastic gradient descent — the "Funk SVD", which is not an SVD at all.

scenes.markdown:
# Learning the vectors: ALS and SGD

## The objective

$$\min_{P,Q}\;\sum_{(u,i)\in\Omega}\big(r_{ui}-q_i^{\top}p_u\big)^2+\lambda\Big(\sum_u\lVert p_u\rVert^2+\sum_i\lVert q_i\rVert^2\Big)$$

Jointly in $(P,Q)$ this is **not convex** (the product $q_i^{\top}p_u$ couples them). But it is quadratic in $P$ for fixed $Q$, and in $Q$ for fixed $P$.

## Alternating least squares

Repeat: for every user, $p_u \leftarrow (Q_{I_u}^{\top}Q_{I_u}+\lambda I)^{-1}Q_{I_u}^{\top}r_u$; then for every movie, $q_i \leftarrow (P_{U_i}^{\top}P_{U_i}+\lambda I)^{-1}P_{U_i}^{\top}r_{\cdot i}$.

- each half-step exactly minimizes over one block, so the objective never increases;
- every user (and every movie) is independent — embarrassingly parallel (Zhou et al., "Large-scale parallel collaborative filtering for the Netflix Prize", 2008);
- the standard solver for implicit feedback (scene 8).

## Stochastic gradient descent

For each observed $(u,i)$: $e_{ui}=r_{ui}-q_i^{\top}p_u$, then

$$q_i\leftarrow q_i+\gamma\,(e_{ui}\,p_u-\lambda\,q_i),\qquad p_u\leftarrow p_u+\gamma\,(e_{ui}\,q_i-\lambda\,p_u).$$

Popularized by Simon Funk's 2006 blog post *"Netflix Update: Try This at Home"* during the Netflix Prize (learning rate 0.001, regularization ≈ 0.02, features trained one at a time). Cheap per update and easy to extend with biases and time effects (Koren et al. 2009).

## In the toy ($k=3$, $\lambda=0.01$, seed 1)

| epoch | 0 | 1 | 2 | 5 | 10 | 50 | 300 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ALS train | 2.75 | 0.63 | 0.07 | 0.013 | 0.013 | 0.007 | 0.006 |
| ALS test | 2.68 | 1.32 | 0.29 | 0.15 | 0.14 | 0.08 | 0.07 |
| SGD test ($\gamma=0.05$) | 2.68 | 1.70 | — | 1.45 | 1.63 | 0.84 | 0.24 |

The hidden ratings come back as 0.97, 4.85, 4.96, 2.97, 2.02, 3.01 against a truth of 1, 5, 5, 3, 2, 3.

## How much data is enough?

A rank-3 $6\times 6$ matrix has 27 degrees of freedom. With 30 observations ALS recovers the hidden cells; hide three more (27 left) and this run collapses. Matrix-completion theory (Candès & Recht, 2009) makes "enough, and spread out" precise for large matrices.

Every number on this page is computed live in your browser by the lesson's domain library, and checked against an independent NumPy implementation.

scenes.markdown:
# Factors aren't genres

## A hidden symmetry

For any invertible $k\times k$ matrix $A$,

$$PQ^{\top} = (PA)\,(QA^{-\top})^{\top}.$$

The objective only ever sees the product, so $(P,Q)$ and $(PA, QA^{-\top})$ fit the data **identically**. A rotation turns users and movies together ($A^{-\top}=A$); a stretch lengthens one side and shortens the other.

## Consequences

- **Learned axes have no names.** The algorithm returns *some* basis of the right subspace. In the toy, the learned factors are $P \approx P^{*}A$ with residual 0.011 — each one a mixture of Action, Romance and Sci-fi.
- **Interpreting factors is a human act.** Koren, Bell & Volinsky (2009, Fig. 3) plot movies on the first two learned factors and *then* describe the directions — lowbrow comedies and horror versus drama with serious undertones, quirky independent films versus mainstream ones; the labels come from inspecting the items, not from the algorithm.
- **Degrees of freedom.** The $k^2$ entries of $A$ are unidentifiable, which is why a rank-$k$ $m\times n$ matrix has $(m+n)k-k^2$ degrees of freedom — 27 for the toy.
- **Regularization breaks part of the symmetry.** With $\lambda>0$, $\lVert PA\rVert^2+\lVert QA^{-\top}\rVert^2$ is not constant in $A$, so the penalty prefers balanced scalings; rotations ($A$ orthogonal) remain free.

## Why it matters

If someone tells you "factor 7 of our model is *horror*", they have labelled it by looking at which items score high on it. A different random seed would produce a different (rotated) factor 7 with the same predictions.

# Tuning, reality, and you

## Capacity: how many factors?

| $k$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| train RMSE, $\lambda=0$ | 1.09 | 0.53 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| test RMSE, $\lambda=0$ | 1.42 | 2.13 | 0.00 | 5.65 | 12.27 |
| test RMSE, $\lambda=0.01$ | 1.42 | 2.12 | 0.07 | 4.15 | 1.06 |

(ALS, 200 epochs, seed 1.) Each user has five known ratings; with five factors the model can fit them exactly *in many ways*, and the one it finds extrapolates badly. Regularization picks the small solution. Real data is noisy, so in practice $\lambda$ also helps at the right $k$; both are tuned on held-out data.

## Biases

Koren, Bell & Volinsky (2009, Eq. 3–4):

$$\hat r_{ui}=\mu+b_u+b_i+q_i^{\top}p_u$$

Their example: $\mu = 3.7$, *Titanic* $b_i = +0.5$, critical Joe $b_u = -0.3$, so the baseline is $3.9$ before any taste matching. In the toy the baseline alone reaches a test RMSE of 1.23, better than user-kNN's 1.61.

## The Netflix Prize (2006–2009)

| milestone | RMSE |
|---|---|
| Cinematch (Oct 2006, quiz set) | 0.9514 |
| Progress Prize 2007 — BellKor (quiz set) | 0.8712 |
| Progress Prize 2008 — BellKor in BigChaos (quiz set) | 0.8616 |
| target (10% better than Cinematch's 0.9525 on the test set) | 0.8572 |
| Grand Prize 2009 — BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos (test set) | 0.8567 |

The winning entry blended over a hundred predictors, mostly factorization variants. Netflix later wrote that it put the Progress-Prize SVD and RBM models into production but not the full Grand-Prize ensemble — the extra accuracy did not justify the engineering cost (Netflix Tech Blog, 2012).

## Fold-in and cold start

A new user is added without retraining by solving one ridge regression against the current item vectors — exactly an ALS half-step. With fewer ratings than factors the system is underdetermined: the **cold-start** problem, handled in practice with biases, popularity, and side information (Koren et al. 2009, Eq. 6, add implicit feedback and user attributes to $p_u$).

**Sources:** Koren, Bell & Volinsky, *IEEE Computer* 2009; Koren, "The BellKor Solution to the Netflix Grand Prize", 2009; Netflix Tech Blog, "Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 stars", 2012.

scenes.markdown:
# Implicit feedback: when there are no stars

## The data

Most recommender data is **implicit**: watches, plays, clicks, purchases, dwell time. It is plentiful, but

- there is **no negative feedback** — dislike shows up only as absence;
- a value says how much, not whether you liked it (Ava watched *Her* once and rated it 2);
- the blanks are **ambiguous**: "would hate it" and "never saw it" look the same.

## Fitting only the positives fails

If every observed cell says "liked", the constant prediction 1 fits perfectly. Scene 4's rule — fit only the known cells — **flips** for implicit data: the blanks must be modelled.

## Preference and confidence (Hu, Koren & Volinsky, ICDM 2008)

$$p_{ui}=\begin{cases}1 & r_{ui}>0\\ 0 & r_{ui}=0\end{cases}\qquad c_{ui}=1+\alpha\,r_{ui}$$

$$\min_{X,Y}\sum_{u,i}c_{ui}\big(p_{ui}-x_u^{\top}y_i\big)^2+\lambda\Big(\sum_u\lVert x_u\rVert^2+\sum_i\lVert y_i\rVert^2\Big)$$

The sum is over **all** pairs. Blanks are zeros with low confidence; heavy use is a one with high confidence. They used $\alpha = 40$ on television viewing data (about 300,000 set-top boxes, 17,000 programs) and also a log-scaled variant, $c_{ui} = 1+\alpha\log(1+r_{ui}/\epsilon)$.

## Weighted ALS

$$x_u=\big(Y^{\top}C^{u}Y+\lambda I\big)^{-1}Y^{\top}C^{u}p(u),\qquad Y^{\top}C^{u}Y = Y^{\top}Y + Y^{\top}(C^{u}-I)Y$$

$Y^{\top}Y$ is shared by all users and $C^{u}-I$ is non-zero only where $u$ interacted, so the cost is linear in the data, not in users × items.

## Evaluation

Implicit recommenders output a **ranking**; they are graded with ranking metrics — Hu et al. used expected percentile rank; precision/recall@K and NDCG are standard. RMSE is meaningless when the targets are 0/1 preferences.

## The same idea everywhere

- **Deep retrieval and two-tower models** (Covington et al., YouTube, RecSys 2016; Yi et al., RecSys 2019): neural networks map users (and, in two-tower models, items) to vectors scored by a dot product, so retrieval is a nearest-neighbor search.
- **word2vec** skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix (Levy & Goldberg, NIPS 2014); *item2vec* (2016) applies it to items.
- **Attention** scores $q^{\top}k$ — see the *Transformer architecture* lesson.
- Rendle, Krichene, Zhang & Anderson (RecSys 2020) showed a well-tuned dot product beats an MLP scorer (NCF) and noted that MLPs struggle to learn a dot product at all.

steps.title: Preference and confidence
steps.description: Hu, Koren & Volinsky (2008) split each cell into a **preference** $p_{ui} \in \{0,1\}$ (watched at all?) and a **confidence** $c_{ui} = 1 + \alpha\, r_{ui}$ (how sure are we?). Blanks become preference 0 with confidence 1; a movie watched six times is preference 1 with confidence $1+6\alpha$.
steps.prompt: Hu et al. used alpha = 40 on TV data (counts in hours-ish units) and also tried a log confidence. alpha sets how much more a watch counts than a non-watch.

steps.title: Weighted ALS over every cell
steps.description:
Now fit **every** cell, weighted by confidence:
$$\min_{X,Y}\sum_{u,i} c_{ui}\big(p_{ui} - x_u^{\top}y_i\big)^2 + \lambda\Big(\sum_u\lVert x_u\rVert^2 + \sum_i \lVert y_i\rVert^2\Big)$$
Each half-step is still a closed form — see the proof, including the trick that keeps it fast. The bottom table is the result. Checked against the star ratings at $\alpha = 10$: Ben's top pick is his best unwatched movie, four others pick one of their tied-best, and Cleo's (*Notebook*, not *Smith*) is wrong.

add.label: weighted-ALS prediction
add.prompt: Weighted ALS over all 36 cells (lambda 0.1, k = 3, 30 iterations). Watched cells ~1, unwatched cells spread out — the ranking among unwatched movies is the recommendation.

steps.prompt: For implicit data the output is a RANKING of unwatched items, evaluated by ranking metrics (Hu et al. used expected percentile rank; precision/recall@K and NDCG are common), not RMSE. On a 6x6 toy those metrics are too noisy to show honestly, so the lesson shows the top picks.

proof.title: Weighted ALS over every cell
proof.goal: Show $x_u = (Y^{\top}C^{u}Y + \lambda I)^{-1}Y^{\top}C^{u}p(u)$, and that $Y^{\top}C^{u}Y = Y^{\top}Y + Y^{\top}(C^{u}-I)Y$ makes it cheap.
proof.prompt: Hu, Koren & Volinsky 2008, Section 4. Weighted ridge regression over ALL items, then the trick that keeps the cost linear in the number of items the user actually touched.

steps.label: The loss for one user, over every item
steps.justification: Hu, Koren & Volinsky (2008), Eq. 3, restricted to the terms containing $x_u$.
steps.explanation: Unlike scene 4, the sum runs over **all** items: unwatched ones are low-confidence zeros.

steps.label: Matrix form
steps.math: J(x_u) = \big(p(u) - Y x_u\big)^{\top} C^{u} \big(p(u) - Y x_u\big) + \lambda\, x_u^{\top} x_u
steps.justification: $C^{u} = \operatorname{diag}(c_{u1},\dots,c_{un})$, $p(u)$ the preference vector, $Y$ the item factors as rows.

steps.label: Gradient to zero
steps.math: \big(Y^{\top} C^{u} Y + \lambda I\big)\, x_u = Y^{\top} C^{u}\, p(u)
steps.explanation: Same shape as the explicit update, with weights.

steps.label: The speed-up
steps.math: Y^{\top} C^{u} Y = \htmlClass{hl-shared}{Y^{\top} Y} + Y^{\top} \htmlClass{hl-sparse}{(C^{u} - I)}\, Y
steps.explanation: Naively each user costs $O(k^2 n)$; with the shared $Y^{\top}Y$ it costs $O(k^2 n_u + k^3)$.

steps.label: The update
steps.math: x_u = \big(Y^{\top}Y + Y^{\top}(C^{u}-I)Y + \lambda I\big)^{-1} Y^{\top} C^{u} p(u)
steps.explanation: Alternate with the mirror-image update for $y_i$. This is the algorithm behind most production "implicit ALS" libraries.

steps.title: Watching is not liking
steps.description: Ava watched *Her* once and gave it 2 stars. To the implicit model that watch is still **preference 1** — at $\alpha = 10$ it predicts **0.90** for her. Raising $\alpha$ only makes it more confident. Confidence weighting says how *sure* we are, not *which way*.

steps.title: Same geometry everywhere
steps.description: The learned vectors live in a factor space again (right). The same idea — embed two kinds of things, score with a dot product — runs through modern ML: deep **retrieval** and **two-tower** models (YouTube 2016, Google 2019), **word2vec**, which implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix (Levy & Goldberg 2014), and the $q^{\top}k$ of **attention**. A well-tuned dot product still holds its own against learned MLP scorers (Rendle et al. 2020).

info.content:
### One idea, many names
- matrix factorization: $q_i^{\top}p_u$
- two-tower retrieval: $f(\text{item})^{\top}g(\text{user})$
- word2vec: $w^{\top}c$
- attention: $q^{\top}k$
